description:
• Background Marine oil spills inflict great damage on marine ecosystems and several times remains un-attributable to the vessel causing such spills. Leveraging satellite imagery along with AIS data will enable detection of oil spills and vessel responsible for the same.
• Description The core challenge attempts to facilitate detection of oil spills and also in identifying the polluting vessel using remote sensing satellite data, such as SAR and EO imagery and AIS data. Participants are to design an intelligent automated pipeline to do the following: (a) Detect and characterise the oil spill and calculating geometric properties and age if feasible. (b) Using oceanographic and meteorological data, it is envisaged to trace the slick towards the origin point and time, predict the future flow of the slick, and (c) analyse and attribute the spill to a vessel using historic AIS data to reconstruct vessel traffic around the origin window in space and time. The irrelevant traffic is to be filtered out and potential suspect vessels are to be scored considering various aspects such as proximity, trajectory, behavioural anomalies etc.
• Expected Solution An automated detection and hindcasting machine learning model that identified oils slicks from satellite imagery, mapping their drift paths backward and forward. It also ranks potential culprit vessel based on spatio-temporal correlation with AIS data. A suitable visual interface is also to be developed.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on machine learning, satellite applied to a space technology problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Space Technology. Tech Depth (3/5): centers on model. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 17/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Satellite Imagery-Based Oil Spill Detection with AIS Data Correlation for Vessel Attribution

overview.in_plain_terms: Build an automated pipeline that detects oil spills at sea from satellite radar images, traces the slick backward to find where and when it started, then cross-references historical ship-tracking data to identify which vessel was likely responsible.
overview.why_it_matters: Marine oil spills currently often go unattributed, meaning the responsible party faces no accountability. Genuine automated detection-plus-attribution changes that.
pain_points: Marine oil spills inflict serious ecological damage but often remain unattributable to the responsible vessel.
No automated pipeline combines spill detection with vessel-traffic reconstruction for attribution.
Manual analysis of satellite imagery and shipping traffic is slow and doesn't scale.
overview.background: Marine oil spills cause significant ecological damage, but attribution to the responsible vessel is often impossible with current manual methods, despite satellite (SAR/EO) imagery and AIS vessel-tracking data both being available.
overview.whats_being_asked: An automated pipeline detecting oil spills from satellite imagery (SAR/EO), hindcasting the slick's origin point/time, and correlating with historical AIS vessel-traffic data to identify and score potential responsible vessels.
expected_solution: Oil spill detection and characterization from SAR/EO imagery.
Oceanographic/meteorological-based slick trajectory hindcasting to origin.
AIS vessel-traffic reconstruction around the origin window.
Suspect vessel scoring based on proximity, trajectory, and behavioral anomalies.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Combining SAR-based spill detection, oceanographic hindcasting, and AIS-based vessel attribution into one automated pipeline is genuine, technically substantial, multi-domain integration.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires SAR image analysis (genuinely different from optical imagery), oceanographic drift modeling, and AIS data correlation together, real cross-domain technical depth.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine remote-sensing (especially SAR), oceanographic modeling, and maritime-domain expertise together, a narrow, technical field.

innovation.note: Genuine end-to-end pipeline connecting detection, hindcasting, and attribution is real, valuable, technically substantial integration.

invention.note: SAR image analysis, oceanographic drift modeling, and AIS correlation together represent significant cross-domain technical depth.

technical_feasibility.note: Public SAR imagery datasets with labeled oil spills exist but are less common than optical datasets; historical AIS data has some public availability but real-time/comprehensive access is limited.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly enables real environmental accountability for a genuinely damaging, often-unaddressed problem.

architecture.note: Detection, hindcasting, and attribution modules integrated into one pipeline, genuine multi-stage architectural complexity.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with real remote-sensing/oceanographic background. Scope your demo to a well-documented historical spill case where SAR imagery and some historical AIS data are accessible, rather than claiming general real-time operational capability.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified, complete pipeline (detection through attribution) with clear, checkable outputs at each stage.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: AIS-based attribution can only score 'potential suspect vessels' probabilistically, never provide definitive proof, this needs honest framing as investigative support, not a legal determination.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Frame your vessel-attribution output explicitly as probabilistic investigative support (a ranked suspect list with confidence scores) rather than a definitive accusation, this is both more honest and more legally appropriate given the real stakes of vessel attribution.

idea_0_4: Source a well-documented historical oil spill case with available SAR imagery for testing.
Research real oceanographic drift/hindcasting methodology and AIS data correlation approaches.
Split: one person on the SAR-based spill detection, one on the hindcasting/AIS-correlation pipeline.
prototype_4_22: Build your SAR-based oil spill detection and characterization model.
Build your oceanographic hindcasting logic tracing the slick toward a probable origin point/time.
Start AIS data correlation, reconstructing vessel traffic around your hindcast origin window.
integration_22_30: Connect detection, hindcasting, and AIS correlation into one coherent pipeline.
Build your suspect-vessel scoring logic based on proximity, trajectory, and behavioral anomaly signals.
Test against your chosen historical case, comparing your pipeline's output against any known/reported findings for that spill.
polish_30_36: Build a clear visualization showing the full pipeline: detected spill, hindcast trajectory, and ranked suspect vessels with confidence scores.
Rehearse presenting your results against your chosen historical validation case.
Prepare to frame your attribution output explicitly as probabilistic investigative support, not definitive proof.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Test your full pipeline against a real, documented historical oil spill case with some known outcome or reported findings, and show your system's detection, hindcast, and suspect-scoring results compared honestly against that real case, that validation against a genuine historical event is the strongest possible evidence for this PS.

strengths: Very well-specified, complete pipeline with clear, checkable stages.
Genuine environmental accountability value for a real, often-unaddressed problem.
weaknesses: Comprehensive real-time AIS data access is limited for a hackathon team, historical case study is the more feasible validation path.
Attribution can only ever be probabilistic, needs careful, honest framing given real legal/accountability stakes.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Weight toward remote-sensing/SAR expertise, that's the more specialized, harder-to-find skill this PS needs.
team_fit.approach: Choose a well-documented historical spill case early, this gives you a concrete validation target for the entire pipeline.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard image-processing pipeline scaffolding and data correlation logic.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly interpreting SAR imagery for spill detection (genuinely different from optical image analysis) and designing scientifically sound oceanographic hindcasting, that requires real remote-sensing and oceanographic domain expertise.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded system without genuine SAR and oceanographic domain grounding could produce confident-looking but scientifically ungrounded hindcast trajectories and vessel attributions, a serious issue given the real accountability stakes.

data_resource_availability.status: Public SAR imagery with some labeled oil spill datasets exists; historical AIS data has some public availability though comprehensive, real-time access is limited.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Focus on a well-documented historical spill case with available SAR imagery and whatever historical AIS data can be sourced, being honest about data completeness limitations.

judge_qna.question: How confident can your system actually be in attributing a spill to a specific vessel, given AIS data limitations?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct that attribution is probabilistic investigative support, a ranked, scored suspect list, not definitive proof, and describe what would be needed for legal-grade attribution beyond your system's output.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your system's behavior when multiple vessels have similarly high suspect scores?

judge_qna.question: How does your oceanographic hindcasting account for real environmental variables like currents and wind that would have been present at the time?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe your specific hindcasting methodology and what oceanographic/meteorological data sources it incorporates, being honest about the accuracy limitations of drift modeling over longer time periods.
judge_qna.follow_up: How does hindcast accuracy degrade the further back in time you trace the slick?
